notes:
THE CONCEPT OF DIVINITY IN ANCIENT TIMES

WHAT THIS CHAPTER COVERS
- Two examples of gods in ancient myths (Zeus from Greece; Thor from Northern Europe).
- Polytheism, with two examples (Hinduism and Shinto).
- The emergence of monotheism (Abraham, Moses, the Covenant).
- The concept of God in Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

KEY TERMS
- Myths of the gods: ancient stories explaining the qualities of gods and goddesses, and advising how to win the gods' favour.
- Archetypes: characteristics that identify a 'type' of god.
- Pantheon: the officially recognised gods of a particular culture.
- Nordic: the countries of Northern Europe - Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Iceland, plus the Faroe Islands, Greenland and Aland.
- Polytheism: belief in many gods.
- Monotheism: belief in one God.
- Moksha: in Hinduism, the end of the cycle of death and rebirth; liberation or enlightenment.
- Atman: Hindu word for 'soul' or 'spirit'.
- Brahman: the ultimate reality or supreme God; also the 'divine consciousness'.
- Puranas: Hindu texts telling the history of the universe from creation to destruction and the family trees of kings, heroes, sages and gods.
- Folk religion: any ethnic or cultural religious practice outside organised religion.
- Kami: the spirits or 'holy powers' venerated (deeply respected) in Shinto.
- Yahweh: the name of the God of ancient Israel, said to have been revealed by Moses.
- Covenant: the agreement between God and the Israelites - God would protect them; they would keep his law and be faithful.
- Idolatry: the worship of false gods.
- Trinity: the Christian belief in God as three persons - Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
- Allah: Arabic for 'God' - not 'a god' but 'the Only God', the Supreme Creator; the main name for God in Islam.
- Qur'an: the central text of Islam, believed to be a revelation from Allah.
- Muhammad: Muslims believe Allah revealed the Qur'an to him in the seventh century CE; he is the final or 'seal' of the prophets.
- Transcendent: belief in a higher power, the other, the sacred - generally called God.

INTRODUCTION
- How did people explain catastrophe? Example: the bubonic plague (the Black Death) in fourteenth-century Europe. Before medical treatment, some saw it as divine punishment and responded with fervent prayer and self-punishment.
- The concept of divinity is common to all religions. From earliest times people believed in God or gods who created the world.
- The idea of God developed as people learned more about the world - from a mythical to a more rational understanding. History and culture shaped it (e.g. the Israelites).
- In patriarchal societies (male/father role dominant), images of God are often male.
- In agricultural societies, God is linked to the land and the seasons.
- In many polytheistic religions there are fertility goddesses, e.g. the Roman goddess Venus, watching over productivity, pregnancy and birth.
- Example image: Barong, king of the spirits in Balinese mythology.

THE GODS OF THE ANCIENTS
- Chapter 4: four types of myth - cosmic, theistic, hero, place/object. This chapter looks at theistic myths (myths of the gods).
- Gods from very different cultures share traits called archetypes, e.g.: father/creator god; great mother; dying god; trickster; destroyer god; helper god; male/female pair; gods who visit the earth and are shunned.
- A pantheon gives insight into the values and mindset of a culture (e.g. the Greek and Egyptian pantheons).

THE GODS OF ANCIENT GREECE
- No common religious text (unlike Christianity, Islam or Hinduism). We learn about them from archaeology - temples and burial sites.
- Greek religion was polytheistic. At its centre were twelve gods and goddesses, the Olympians, in a hierarchy with Zeus, king of the gods, at the top.
- The gods had human flaws: vanity, jealousy, anger. They were often cruel, fickle (changeable), vindictive, jealous and insecure - yet immortal with special powers, which they used over each other and humans for revenge or pleasure.
- If something good happened, you had pleased a god; if bad, you had displeased them (or caught them on a bad day).
THE TWELVE OLYMPIANS
- Zeus - leader of the family of gods.
- Hera - Zeus's wife, goddess of marriage.
- Ares - god of war.
- Artemis - goddess of wild beasts and hunting.
- Poseidon - god of the sea and earthquakes.
- Athena - goddess of war and wisdom.
- Aphrodite - goddess of love and beauty.
- Hermes - messenger of the gods, god of travellers.
- Demeter - goddess of agriculture and harvest.
- Hephaestus - god of fire and metalworking.
- Apollo - god of music, poetry and art.
- Hestia - goddess of the hearth and family life.
- Gods were tied to cities: Athena with Athens; Zeus with Olympia, where the Olympic Games were held in his honour.
- People turned to specific gods for specific needs: Hera for weddings, Ares for war.
- Festivals every four years at Olympia, Delphi, Nemea and Isthmia - feasting, sacrifice and athletic competitions.
- Good fortune (e.g. a good marriage match) came from pleasing the gods; bad fortune (extreme weather, disasters) from displeasing them, from the gods' arbitrary (random) treatment, or bad luck.
- The Iliad and the play Oedipus the King both begin with plagues presented as punishments, not freak events.
- Life must have felt insecure - the gods were unpredictable and hard to please.
- Quotes: Alexander Pope - 'The united strength of all the gods above. In vain resists the omnipotence of Jove [Zeus].' Virgil - Athena 'hurled Jupiter's swift fire from the clouds, scattered the ships, and made the sea boil with storms.'

ZEUS: THE FATHER OF HEAVEN
- The ancient gods were feared rather than loved.
- Zeus: strong and powerful, father, husband, head of the family, but with the failings of a mortal man. A sky god concerned with the weather; his weapon was the thunderbolt.
- Myth adapted from The Greek Myths by Robert Graves:
- Only Zeus could wield the thunderbolt; he used its threat to control his quarrelsome family on Mount Olympus. He ordered the heavenly bodies, made laws, enforced oaths and pronounced oracles.
- Hera equalled him in one thing only: she could give the gift of prophecy to any man or beast.
- Zeus's pride and petulance (childishness) became intolerable. Hera, Poseidon, Apollo and all the Olympians except Hestia tied him up while he slept with rawhide thongs in a hundred knots, put his thunderbolt out of reach and laughed at him.
- While they argued about who would succeed him, Thetis the Nereid, foreseeing civil war, fetched the hundred-handed Briareus, who untied him using every hand at once.
- Punishment: Hera, the leader, was hung from the sky with a golden bracelet on each wrist and an anvil on each ankle. Zeus freed her only when all swore never to rebel again.
- Poseidon and Apollo were sent as bond-servants to King Laomedon, for whom they built the city of Troy. The others were pardoned as acting under duress.

THE GODS OF NORTHERN AND WESTERN EUROPE
- Gods of thunder, rain and wind - probably reflecting the colder, darker climate; culture shapes how people see gods.
- Nordic mythology shows a constant struggle against darkness and chaos; gods fight giants and monsters (forces of evil).
- Odin: father of the Norse gods; one eye; fierce in battle, wise in peace; rides across the sky on an eight-legged horse.

THE STORY OF THOR ('THE LAY OF THRYM')
- Thor: god of thunder, son of Odin; huge, red-bearded; armed with a hammer, iron gloves and a girdle of strength; outspoken, with an enormous appetite for food and drink.
- Thor wakes to find his hammer missing; so angry his hands tremble and beard shakes.
- With his henchman Loki he asks the goddess Freyja to lend Loki her wings to fly to Jotunheim, land of the giants.
- Thrym, king of the giants, boasts he hid the hammer seven leagues under the earth and will return it only if he gets Freyja as his bride. Freyja is furious.
- The god Heimdall's plan: Thor dresses as the bride (hair tied up, two stones under his tunic). Thor reluctantly agrees.
- At the feast Thor eats a whole ox and eight salmon and drinks three barrels of beer. Loki explains 'Freyja' had not eaten for a week from excitement.
- Thrym lifts the veil and sees Thor's burning eyes; Loki says the bride had not slept for a week.
- Thrym orders the hammer laid in the bride's lap; Thor laughs, kills Thrym and wipes out all the giants and their kin. A happy ending for the gods.
- Meaning: Nordic people used it to explain what they did not understand - the lost hammer may explain crop failure or drought; getting it back may symbolise the coming of spring.
- Jostein Gaarder, Sophie's World: a myth was not only an explanation - people carried out religious ceremonies related to myths, e.g. acting out a drama of the myth during drought or crop failure.

TWO FURTHER GREEK MYTHS (EXTRA)
- Narcissus (classic version by the Roman poet Ovid in Metamorphoses): his mother Liriope was told by the seer Tiresias that he would live long if he never saw his reflection. The nymph Echo loved him; he rejected her and she faded until only an echo remained. Nemesis, goddess of revenge, lured him to a pool; he fell in love with his own reflection, withered away in despair and became a gold and white flower. Narcissism = fixation with oneself, one's appearance or public image (discussion: social media and young people).
- Sisyphus: King of Corinth, famous for trickery; cheated death and Hades (god of the underworld) twice; Homer in The Iliad called him 'the most cunning of men'. Zeus punished him to roll a boulder up a hill for all eternity; it always rolls back down. Symbol of the foolishness of trying to escape mortality. 'Sisyphean' = a task that can never be completed.
- Conclusion: around the fifth century BCE the Greeks began thinking in a new way - philosophers Socrates, Plato and Aristotle broke from the mythic view (Chapter 2).

POLYTHEISM
- Belief in many gods. Many world religions today are polytheistic; the three great exceptions - the classical monotheistic religions - are Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
- Both monotheism and polytheism are ways of understanding the transcendent (the higher power, the other, the sacred - God).

HINDUISM
- The world's third-largest religion; often presented as polytheistic.
- Began as a collection of beliefs and practices; originated in India around 3500 BCE in the Indus Valley Civilisation; no single founder.
- Holy men called rishis meditated alone in caves in the Himalayas, open to revealed truths. They wrote sacred verses/hymns, collected into four books called the Vedas.
- The Puranas: sacred text telling the story of creation and the lives of the gods.
- Goal: moksha - liberation, release from the cycle of birth, death and rebirth.
- Each person has a soul, the atman, which can be born millions of times in millions of forms (incarnations). Freed from worldly attachments only by living good lives in each life.
- Ultimate goal: to be delivered into eternity - Brahman, the godhead, source and origin of all creation; a distant, all-powerful god approached through more accessible deities:
- Brahma - the creator, brings the universe into existence.
- Vishnu - preserves life and all living things.
- Shiva - destroys the world.
- This Hindu trinity represents the cycle of creation, preservation and destruction, the centre of Hindu belief. The goddess Mahadeiri (as spelled in the textbook) is also a principal deity.
- Hinduism combines two ways of seeing God: it looks polytheistic, but the gods are manifestations of the one God. Brahman mirrors the God of monotheism, but unlike monotheism Hinduism has lesser gods with human characteristics who are more accessible.
- Hindus often have a favourite deity with a shrine at home.
- Four stages to reach moksha: 1. student (learn sacred literature); 2. householder (responsibility in society); 3. contemplative (reflect and meditate); 4. ascetic (renounce worldly pleasures).
WORSHIP IN HINDUISM
- Puja: worship, usually personal rather than communal, in temple or home. Offerings of fruit, water or flowers; prayers as mantras.
- Most homes have a shrine (a room, image or statue) regarded as sacred space; families pray together, three times a day when possible.
- Pilgrimage to rivers, mountains, temples and sacred sites in India where gods may have appeared.
- Kumbh Mela: every twelve years, up to ten million people gather where the Ganges and Yamuna meet; ritual bathing to wash away sins. The Ganges (India and Bangladesh) is the holy river.
- Varanasi, on the Ganges: believed to be Lord Shiva's home. Hindus who die there have ashes scattered on the Ganges - the best death possible.

SHINTO
- Japanese religion from prehistoric Japan; no founder and no particular doctrine; practised as a folk religion, often alongside Buddhism.
- Efforts in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries to remove Buddhist influence led to 'State Shinto' around 1868. Shinto lost its status as Japan's official religion in 1945.
- Name coined in the sixth century CE from Chinese shen ('divine being') and tao ('way') - 'the way of the gods'.
- Gods/spirits are kami, with special powers; legend says the gods who controlled the cosmos came down and lived in mountains, streams, rocks and special parts of the landscape.
- Amaterasu, the sun goddess, is the supreme deity, worshipped at the Ise Grand Shrine. She is the daughter of Izanagi, a creator god with his sister and lover Izanami.
- Worship at shrines called jinja with very precise rituals; shamans make sure rituals are done correctly. Believers ask kami for favours and blessings.
- Purpose: to know and carry out the wishes of the kami; each day is a chance for service (matsumi).
- Positive view of the person: humans and nature are children of the kami and fundamentally good; rituals cleanse the person so this goodness shows.
- Shinto and anime: characters visit shrines, receive charms (amulets), light incense for the dead; themes of nature and healing. Spirited Away (Oscar-winning) has many Shinto references. Pokemon creator Satoshi Tajiri drew on Japan's religious history; Pokemon can be seen as representations of kami - some friendly, some threatening.

THE EMERGENCE OF MONOTHEISM AND GOD IN JUDAISM
- The concept of one God first emerged in Judaism. The move from polytheism to monotheism was slow and often confused, and changed ritual and worship.
- Abraham is the man mainly associated with this move. He lived between 2000 and 1500 BCE in the Fertile Crescent (ancient Near East), stretching from Mesopotamia to Egypt. Canaan was the fertile land between them; many nomads, including Abraham, came seeking a settled life.
- Genesis 11:31: Abraham, his father Terah, wife Sarah and nephew Lot left Ur in Mesopotamia for Canaan; settled in Haran until Terah died; Abraham became leader.
- Genesis 12: 'Go from your country and your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you.' Promise: 'I will bless you, and make your name great ... in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed' (Gn 12:1-3).
- At Shechem in Canaan: 'To your offspring I will give this land' (Gn 12:7). Abraham built an altar - the start of the special relationship between God and the Israelites.
- Genesis and Exodus show their struggle to believe in one God in a culture full of many gods.
- Exodus (final chapters written fifth century BCE): God's covenant with Moses on Mount Sinai. The very idea of a covenant shows polytheism was still alive - the people promised to worship Yahweh alone.
- At first the Israelites seem to have thought Yahweh was one god among others; through the covenant they pledged loyalty to Yahweh alone. The Pentateuch (first five books of the Old Testament) assumes other gods exist.
- Ten Commandments: 'I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery; you shall have no other gods before me' (Deut 5:6-7).
- At the heart of the covenant: a caring God, like a father to his children. 'I will be your God and you will be my people' (Ex 6:7).

GOD IN CHRISTIANITY
- Comes from the Jewish God of the Old Testament; Jesus of Nazareth was a Jew. Christians and Jews share belief in an all-powerful creator God and the Genesis creation stories.
- God is beyond full human understanding, yet wants to be known as loving and caring, creator and sustainer of all. 'God is love' (1 John 4:8).
- God reveals himself through creation, the Old Testament prophets, and mainly through his Son, Jesus - God became flesh in Jesus, the divine-human Son of God.
- Jesus' life, death and resurrection reveal God uniquely; this revelation is a saving event.
- After the ascension, God communicates through the Holy Spirit, who descended on the disciples at Pentecost.
- The Trinity: one God in three persons - Father, Son and Holy Spirit - each equally divine; only the Son became incarnate ('enfleshed'). The Trinity is a community of divine persons, the model community of love.
- Formalised at the Council of Nicaea in 325 and expressed in the Nicene Creed ('I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth ... one Lord Jesus Christ, the Only Begotten Son of God ... consubstantial with the Father ... the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the giver of life').
- A personal God who loves and wants love in return; forgiving and merciful.
- Abba: the word Jesus used for God - an intimate father-child term like 'dad' or 'daddy'.
- God's tenderness can also be shown through the image of motherhood; God is neither man nor woman.

GOD IN ISLAM
- Allah is believed to be the same God worshipped by Jews and Christians; Allah is Arabic for God; Arab Christians also say Allah.
- The oneness of God is central.
- The Qur'an contains the Word of God revealed to Muhammad, the great prophet, in the seventh century; the ultimate source of Allah's revelation; through it Muslims know Allah's will.
- God is so great and 'otherworldly' that humans will never fully know him. Allah is creator of all, the All-Powerful, revealed through the world and the Qur'an.
- Allah is merciful (the word is used extensively in the Qur'an) and generous, All Great and Most Just. On the Last Day Allah will judge people on their words and actions.
- 'Islam' means total submission and surrender to the will of God; the Qur'an is the blueprint for submission and salvation.
- Qur'an 59:22-24: 'He is God: there is no god but He ... the all-Merciful, the all-Compassionate ... the Creator, the Maker, the Shaper. To him belongs the Names Most Beautiful.'
THE FIVE PILLARS OF ISLAM
- 1. Shahada (declaration of faith): there is one God (Allah) worthy of worship and Muhammad is his messenger. Saying it makes a person a Muslim.
- 2. Salat (prayer): five times a day - before sunrise, after midday, afternoon, after sunset, bedtime; in Arabic; at home, elsewhere or in the mosque; standing, bowing, prostrating, reciting the Qur'an; facing Mecca (Saudi Arabia).
- 3. Zakat (charity): 'almsgiving' or 'poor tax' - 2.5% of wealth above a threshold to the poor; a way of thanking Allah; cares for the worldwide Muslim community.
- 4. Sawm (fasting): no food or drink in daylight during Ramadan, the ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar (moves forward eight or nine days each year). Purpose: greater consciousness of God, gratitude, compassion for those with less; spiritual reflection and self-control.
- 5. Hajj (pilgrimage): to Mecca at least once for all physically and financially able. Mecca is home of the Ka'aba and birthplace of Muhammad. The Ka'aba is believed built by Abraham (Ibrahim) and one of his sons; restored by Muhammad as the focus of worship. Over two million attend each year, all in the same white garments to show equality.

SUMMARY
- Theistic myths tried to capture the idea of god for ancient peoples.
- Polytheism is seen in Hinduism and Shinto.
- Monotheism gradually emerged in the time of Abraham.
- The three great monotheistic religions: Judaism, Christianity, Islam.
- Exam tip: excellent answers go beyond the content - deeper knowledge, research, links between topics and real engagement.

rows.prompt: How did some people explain the Black Death in the fourteenth century?
options: As a disease spread by rats
As a sign of the coming spring
rows.explanation: Before medical treatment existed, some saw the plague as divine punishment and responded with prayer and self-punishment.

rows.prompt: In agricultural societies, how are images of God usually understood?
options: Linked to the land and the seasons
rows.explanation: The chapter says in agricultural societies God is linked to the land and the cycle of the seasons.

rows.prompt: What is a pantheon?
options: A temple where all gods are worshipped
A type of god, such as a trickster
The officially recognised gods of a culture
rows.explanation: A pantheon is the officially recognised set of gods of a particular culture.

rows.prompt: Characteristics that identify a 'type' of god, like the trickster, are called what?
rows.explanation: Archetypes are shared characteristics that identify a type of god, e.g. father/creator, great mother, trickster.

rows.prompt: How many Olympian gods and goddesses were at the centre of Greek religion?
rows.explanation: At the centre were twelve gods and goddesses known as the Olympians.

rows.prompt: Who was the Greek goddess of marriage?
rows.explanation: Hera, Zeus's wife, was goddess of marriage; Greeks turned to her for weddings.

rows.prompt: Which goddess was closely associated with the city of Athens?
rows.explanation: Athena, goddess of war and wisdom, was closely associated with Athens.

rows.prompt: How do we mainly learn about the gods of ancient Greece?
options: A single sacred text like the Bible
Archaeological finds like temples and burial sites
rows.explanation: The Greeks had no common religious text, so archaeology helps us understand their gods.

rows.prompt: How do the Iliad and Oedipus the King present plagues?
options: As catastrophic punishments from the gods
As signs of a new season
rows.explanation: Both begin with plagues presented as punishments rather than freak events.

rows.prompt: What was Zeus's weapon?
rows.explanation: Zeus was a sky god and only he could wield the thunderbolt.

rows.prompt: Which Olympian did NOT join the plot to tie up Zeus?
rows.explanation: All the Olympians except Hestia surrounded and bound Zeus as he slept.

rows.prompt: Who freed Zeus after he was tied up?
rows.explanation: Thetis fetched Briareus, who untied the hundred knots using every hand at once.

He made them bond-servants who built Troy
He chained them to a pillar
He banished them to the underworld

rows.prompt: Thor was the Norse god of what?
rows.explanation: Thor was the god of thunder and the son of Odin.

rows.prompt: Who suggested that Thor dress up as a bride?
rows.explanation: The god Heimdall came up with the plan for Thor to dress as Freyja.

rows.prompt: What might Thor getting his hammer back have symbolised for Nordic people?
rows.explanation: The loss of the hammer may explain drought or crop failure; its return may symbolise spring.

rows.prompt: What is moksha in Hinduism?
options: Release from the cycle of birth, death and rebirth
rows.explanation: Moksha is liberation - the end of the cycle of birth, death and rebirth.

rows.prompt: Which Hindu god preserves life and all living things?
rows.explanation: Brahma creates, Vishnu preserves and Shiva destroys.

rows.prompt: What is the Hindu word for the soul?
rows.explanation: Each person has a soul, the atman, which can be reborn many times.

rows.prompt: Why can Hinduism be seen as both polytheistic and monotheistic?
options: It has one god for each region of India
It rejects all gods except Shiva
Its many gods are manifestations of one God
It borrowed its gods from Shinto
rows.explanation: Hinduism appears polytheistic, but its gods are manifestations of the one God, Brahman.

rows.prompt: Where does the Kumbh Mela take place?
options: Where the Ganges and Yamuna rivers meet
In the caves of the Himalayas

rows.explanation: Shinto comes from shen ('divine being') and tao ('way') - the way of the gods.

As fundamentally good, a child of the kami

To show all pilgrims are equal

rows.prompt: Describe the character of the gods of ancient Greece.
rows.model_answer: The Greek gods were immortal and had great powers, but they also had human flaws such as vanity, jealousy and anger. They were often cruel, fickle, vindictive and insecure, and used their powers for revenge or pleasure. People feared rather than loved them, and life felt insecure because the gods were unpredictable and hard to please.

rows.prompt: What does the myth of the Olympians' rebellion tell us about Zeus?
rows.model_answer: It shows Zeus was the most powerful god, controlling his family with the thunderbolt, making laws and pronouncing oracles. But it also shows his human failings: his pride and petulance were so bad that the gods tied him up. When freed he was cruel and vengeful, hanging Hera from the sky and sending Poseidon and Apollo to build Troy as bond-servants.

rows.prompt: Explain what questions the myth of Thor's hammer may have answered for Nordic people.
rows.model_answer: Thor was the god of thunder with a huge appetite, so the loss of his hammer may have explained drought or crop failure. His getting the hammer back may have symbolised the coming of spring. As Sophie's World says, people may also have acted out the myth in religious ceremonies at times of drought.

rows.prompt: Name the three principal deities of Hinduism and say what each does.
rows.model_answer: Brahma is the creator who brings the universe into existence. Vishnu preserves life and all living things. Shiva destroys the world. Together they represent the cycle of creation, preservation and destruction, which is at the centre of Hindu belief.

rows.prompt: Name the four stages a Hindu must go through to achieve moksha.
rows.model_answer: First is being a student, to learn about the sacred literature. Second is being a householder, to develop responsibility in society. Third is being a contemplative, to reflect and meditate on important things in life. Fourth is being an ascetic, giving up the pleasures of the world.

rows.prompt: Explain why Shinto is described as a polytheistic religion.
rows.model_answer: Shinto believes in many gods or spirits called kami, which have special powers. Legend says the gods came down to Earth and live in mountains, streams, rocks and special parts of the landscape. Amaterasu, the sun goddess, is the supreme deity, and believers worship many kami at shrines called jinja, asking them for favours and blessings.

rows.prompt: Explain why the move from polytheism to monotheism in Judaism 'did not happen overnight'.
rows.model_answer: The change was slow and often confused. Abraham began a special relationship with one God, but the Israelites lived among peoples who believed in many gods and seem at first to have seen Yahweh as one god among others. Even in Exodus, the covenant at Mount Sinai required them to promise to worship Yahweh alone, and the Ten Commandments say 'you shall have no other gods before me', showing other gods were still assumed to exist.

rows.prompt: Explain the Christian belief in the Trinity.
rows.model_answer: Christians believe in one God in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Each person is equally divine, but only the Son, Jesus, became incarnate. The Trinity is a community of divine persons, the model community of love. This belief was formalised at the Council of Nicaea and expressed in the Nicene Creed.

rows.prompt: Profile the understanding of God/the gods that can be seen in two myths from ancient times which you have studied.
rows.model_answer:
In the Greek myth of Zeus, adapted from Robert Graves' The Greek Myths, Zeus is the Father of Heaven and king of the twelve Olympians. He alone wields the thunderbolt, orders the heavenly bodies, makes laws and pronounces oracles. Yet he has the failings of a mortal man: his pride and petulance become so bad that Hera, Poseidon, Apollo and the others (except Hestia) tie him up in a hundred knots. Freed by the hundred-handed Briareus, he takes cruel revenge, hanging Hera from the sky with anvils on her ankles and sending Poseidon and Apollo to build Troy. This shows gods who were powerful but fickle, vengeful and feared rather than loved.

In the Nordic myth 'The Lay of Thrym', Thor, god of thunder and son of Odin, loses his hammer to Thrym, king of the giants, who demands the goddess Freyja as his bride. Thor dresses as the bride, eats an ox and eight salmon, then kills Thrym and all the giants. Thor is strong, hot-tempered and has a huge appetite, and the gods are shown in constant struggle against forces of chaos. The myth may explain drought or crop failure and the coming of spring.

In both myths the gods are human-like, powerful and violent, reflecting the cultures that created them.

rows.prompt: Explain polytheism and give two examples of polytheistic religions.
rows.model_answer:
Polytheism is the belief in many gods. Many world religions today are polytheistic; the three great exceptions are the monotheistic religions of Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

Hinduism, the world's third-largest religion, began in India around 3500 BCE in the Indus Valley Civilisation and has no single founder. Its sacred texts include the Vedas and the Puranas. Hindus seek moksha, release from the cycle of birth, death and rebirth, so that the atman (soul) can return to Brahman, the godhead and source of all creation. Brahman is approached through more accessible gods: Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver and Shiva the destroyer. Hindus worship through puja, offering fruit, water or flowers at home shrines, and go on pilgrimage, such as the Kumbh Mela on the Ganges. Although Hinduism looks polytheistic, its gods are manifestations of one God.

Shinto, 'the way of the gods', comes from prehistoric Japan and has no founder or doctrine. It believes in many kami, spirits who live in mountains, streams and rocks. The supreme deity is Amaterasu, the sun goddess, worshipped at the Ise Grand Shrine. Worship takes place at shrines called jinja with precise rituals overseen by shamans, and believers ask the kami for blessings.

rows.prompt: Profile one example of how a monotheistic understanding of God developed in a context where polytheism was widespread.
rows.model_answer:
Monotheism, belief in one God, first emerged in Judaism. Abraham, who lived between 2000 and 1500 BCE in the Fertile Crescent, is the person mainly associated with the move from polytheism to monotheism. Genesis 11:31 tells us that Abraham, his father Terah, wife Sarah and nephew Lot left Ur in Mesopotamia and settled in Haran. After Terah died, the Lord told Abraham, 'Go from your country ... to the land that I will show you', and promised to bless him and make his name great (Gn 12:1-3). At Shechem in Canaan God promised, 'To your offspring I will give this land', and Abraham built an altar. This began the special relationship between God and the Israelites.

The change was slow and confused because the surrounding culture believed in many gods. At first the Israelites seem to have seen Yahweh as one god among others. In Exodus, God made a covenant with Moses on Mount Sinai: God would protect them and they would worship Yahweh alone. The Ten Commandments say, 'you shall have no other gods before me' (Deut 5:6-7), which shows other gods were still assumed to exist. At the heart of the covenant is a caring God, like a father: 'I will be your God and you will be my people' (Ex 6:7).

rows.prompt: Explain the concept of God in Islam, with reference to the Five Pillars.
rows.model_answer:
The God of Islam is Allah, the Arabic word for God, meaning not 'a god' but 'the Only God'. Muslims believe Allah is the same God worshipped by Jews and Christians. The oneness of God is central. Allah revealed the Qur'an to Muhammad, the final prophet, in the seventh century, and it is the ultimate source of his revelation. Allah is so great and 'otherworldly' that humans can never fully know him. He is creator of all, All-Powerful, merciful, generous and Most Just, and will judge people on the Last Day. 'Islam' means total submission to God's will.

The Five Pillars show this understanding. The Shahada declares there is one God and Muhammad is his messenger. Salat, prayer five times a day facing Mecca, shows constant devotion to God. Zakat, giving 2.5% of wealth to the poor, is a way of thanking Allah for his goodness. Sawm, fasting in daylight during Ramadan, builds consciousness of God. The Hajj to Mecca, where all wear white, shows that all are equal before God.
